consensus_summary: Blind responses converge on lamp oil as primarily symbolizing the Holy Spirit (His presence, empowering grace, and illumination that sustains light and readiness), drawing on Zechariah 4, sanctuary oil for perpetual lamps, anointing texts, and popular readings of the ten virgins; alternatives such as mere readiness, good works/charity, saving faith, or grace are noted as common or minority but secondary, with no fully settled consensus.
book_summary: Oil is the pressed, tested fruit of the olive: the fruit and evidence of the Spirit’s work made manifest in proven obedience, stored and burned to produce light; it is explicitly not the Spirit Himself.
rationale: The book’s central claim displaces the dominant consensus identification of oil with the Holy Spirit by denying that equation and relocating the symbol to the Spirit’s outward fruit in tested obedience; while this overlaps some alternative readings (good works, proven faith), the explicit contradiction of the primary common view makes the relation divergent rather than refined or matching.
strongest_objection: Zechariah 4 and the broader anointing motif so tightly link oil-fed lamps with the Spirit that any reading insisting ‘not the Spirit Himself’ appears forced, and the ten-virgins oil is better left unallegorized beyond readiness.
